stem: What is the main feature of an **enterprise resource planning (ERP)** system?

options.content: A single database shared by all
options.rationale: Correct: sales, stock, production and finance all use the same up-to-date information.

options.content: A separate record for each department
options.rationale: Separate records are what ERP replaces.

options.content: A system that replaces all managers
options.rationale: ERP provides information to managers; it does not replace them.
That describes marketing software, not ERP.

explanation: ERP links the main functions of the business through a single database so that information is entered once and shared.

stem: What does **CAD** stand for in operations?

options.rationale: Correct: computers are used to create and test designs.
CAD is about design, not delivery.
This is not the meaning of CAD.
This is not the meaning of CAD.

explanation: CAD is computer-aided design. CAM, computer-aided manufacturing, uses computers to control the machines that make the product.

stem: Which benefit of computerised **inventory control** is most direct?

options.content: Stock never needs to be counted
options.rationale: Occasional counts are still needed to check the records.

options.content: Stock levels are known at once
options.rationale: Correct: stock is recorded as it moves, so managers can see what is held.
A computer system cannot make suppliers deliver on time.
Prices to customers are not changed by the stock system.

explanation: Computerised control records stock as it is received and issued, so levels are always up to date and low stock can be spotted early.
hints: Think about what the computer records and when.

stem: Which of these is a typical **limitation** of introducing an integrated computer system?

options.rationale: A good system makes information more accurate, provided the data entered is correct.

options.content: Costs of every kind fall straight away
options.rationale: The system itself costs money to buy and install.
Computer systems depend on power.

options.content: Staff need training and may resist
options.rationale: Correct: users must learn new methods, and some staff dislike change.

explanation: Training, resistance and disruption are common costs of a new system, in addition to its price.
hints: Think of the people who must use the system.

stem: A fictional hardware wholesaler in Harare uses ERP. When a customer's order is entered, the stock module shows that cement is below its reorder level and a purchase order is raised. Which area of operations does this **most directly** improve?

options.rationale: The example is about stock, not designing products.
Branding is a marketing matter and is not concerned here.
Wage negotiation is unrelated to the stock link described.
Correct: the system links sales to stock and triggers ordering before a shortage.

explanation: Linking sales and stock lets the business order materials in time, reducing stock-outs and excess stock.
hints: What does the system do once the order is entered?

stem: A fictional timber merchant in Mutare estimates that a stock and costing system will lower its stock held from US\$50,000 to US\$38,000 (holding cost 15% a year), save 1,200 hours of clerical work at US\$2.50 an hour and avoid US\$4,200 of lost sales a year. What are the total annual benefits?

options.rationale: That leaves out the holding-cost saving.
That adds the whole fall in stock (US\$12,000) instead of the holding-cost saving.
That leaves out the saving in clerical work.

explanation: Holding cost saved = 12,000 × 15% = 1,800. Clerical saving = 1,200 × 2.50 = 3,000. Lost sales avoided = 4,200. Total = US\$9,000.
hints: Only the holding cost of the stock saved is a yearly benefit.

stem: A fictional furniture factory has ERP, but its storekeeper often forgets to record issues of timber. What is the most likely effect?

options.content: Costs of timber will fall automatically
options.rationale: Wrong records do not reduce costs; they cause errors.

options.content: The ERP system will correct the errors itself
options.rationale: The system cannot know about issues that are never recorded.
Correct: the system relies on accurate data, so errors spread to ordering and costing.
Supplier speed is not affected by internal recording.

explanation: ERP is only as good as the data entered. Unrecorded issues make stock records wrong, which leads to wrong orders and wrong job costs.
hints: What does an integrated system depend on?

stem: A fictional small tuck shop with two staff and a single product line is offered a full ERP package at a high price. Which is the best reason for **not** buying it?

options.rationale: Computers hold stock records well.

options.content: Costs are likely to exceed benefits
options.rationale: Correct: a very small business would use little of the system and gain little from linking functions.

options.content: ERP can only ever be used by large factories
options.rationale: It is not true that ERP can only be used by large factories; small ones often use parts of it.
Customers are not concerned with internal records.

explanation: The benefits of integration grow with size and complexity. For a tiny shop a simple stock program may give most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.
hints: Compare the cost with the benefits a very small business could gain.

stem: Computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) uses computers to control the machines that make a product.
explanation: True. CAM uses computers to control machines and the process of manufacture; CAD is used for the design stage.

stem: A computerised system removes the need for accurate data to be entered by staff.
explanation: False. The system depends on the data entered. If staff record stock or costs wrongly, the reports will be wrong.

stem: Match each ICT tool or term to its use.

right.content: Recording stock as it is received and issued
Recording costs of each job as they arise
Creating and testing product designs on screen
Controlling machines that make the product

explanation: Each tool applies computers to a different part of operations.

stem: Choose the correct word for each gap.

payload.template: An ERP system uses a single {{blank:a}} that is shared by all departments, so information needs to be entered only {{blank:b}}.

explanation: ERP stores information in one shared database, entered once and used by every department.

stem: State **one** way in which computerised costing can help a manufacturer.
explanation: Accept: more accurate and up-to-date costs for each job or product, better prices, time saved, fewer errors, or easier cost control.

stem: A fictional clothing factory in Gweru buys a computerised stock and costing system for US\$16,000 plus US\$3,500 for installation and training. It expects annual benefits of US\$8,200 and pays a support fee of US\$1,300 a year. Benefits arise evenly through each year. Calculate the payback period in years, to two decimal places.
explanation: Outlay = 16,000 + 3,500 = US\$19,500. Net annual benefit = 8,200 - 1,300 = US\$6,900. Payback = 19,500 ÷ 6,900 = 2.83 years. Ignoring the support fee gives 2.38 years.
hints: Use the net annual benefit after the support fee.

stem: A fictional bakery chain in Bulawayo holds average stock of US\$40,000. Its new computerised stock control is expected to cut stock by 30%, and holding stock costs 15% of its value a year. Calculate the annual saving in holding costs.
hints: Find 30% of the stock first, then 15% of that.

stem: Explain what is meant by enterprise resource planning (ERP).

points.description: Software that links the main functions of a business
Through a single database that all departments share
So that information is entered once and everyone uses up-to-date data

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: ERP is software that links functions such as sales, stock, production and finance through one database shared by all departments, so information is entered once and everyone works with up-to-date data.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: Say what is linked and how.

stem: A fictional bakery in Masvingo has separate stock records for flour, sugar and packaging. Explain two ways in which a computerised stock system could help it.

points.description: It records stock as it is used, so levels are always up to date
Application: the baker knows when flour is low and can order before running out
It can give a warning when stock reaches the reorder level
Application: avoids baking being stopped and reduces over-ordering of sugar that may go hard

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The system records stock as it is used, so the baker always knows how much flour is left and can order before running out. It can also warn when stock reaches the reorder level, which avoids stopping baking and stops over-ordering of sugar that may go hard.

explanation: Two ways, each applied.
hints: Link each way to flour, sugar or packaging.

stem: Analyse how better management information from an ERP system could improve pricing decisions.

points.description: Costs of each product or job are recorded accurately
The manager knows the true cost of making each item
Prices can be set to give the profit wanted and not below cost
Reports on sales and demand show which items can bear a higher price

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The system records the costs of each product accurately, so the manager knows the true cost of making each item. Prices can then be set to give the profit wanted and avoid selling below cost. Reports on sales also show which items can bear a higher price.

explanation: One point per mark.
hints: Follow the chain from accurate cost to price.

stem: A fictional furniture factory with 35 workers in Bulawayo is considering an ERP system. Evaluate whether it should buy one.

points.description: It links orders, stock and production, reducing stock-outs and late deliveries
Accurate costing helps set better prices
The cost of buying, installing and training is high for a 35-worker business
Power failures and poor data can stop the system or mislead managers
Counter-argument: modules can be introduced one at a time to spread the cost
Judgement with a reason, for example buy the stock and costing modules first with a back-up power supply

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An ERP system would link orders, stock and production, reducing stock-outs and late deliveries, and accurate costs would help set better prices. But buying, installing and training staff is expensive for a business with 35 workers, and power failures or poor data could stop the system or mislead managers. The modules can be introduced one at a time. The factory should start with the stock and costing modules and make sure there is a back-up power supply.

explanation: One point per mark; the judgement needs a reason.
hints: Weigh the benefits against cost and the conditions in which the factory works.

stem: A fictional building-materials supplier in Chinhoyi spends US\$5,400 a year on clerical staff to prepare orders and invoices by hand. A computerised system would cut this work by two thirds, but its software costs US\$7,200 and training US\$1,800.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual saving in clerical costs.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period in years, to two decimal places, if the only benefit is the saving in clerical costs.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain two benefits other than the saving in cost that the supplier could gain from the system.

points.description: Orders and invoices are produced faster and with fewer errors
Application: customers receive correct invoices sooner, which may reduce late payments
Stock records are always up to date
Application: the supplier knows when cement or paint is low and can order in time
Better information for managers on sales and stock

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Orders and invoices are produced faster and with fewer errors, so customers receive correct invoices sooner and may pay on time. Stock records are always up to date, so the supplier knows when cement or paint is low and can order in time, avoiding lost sales.

explanation: Saving US\$3,600 a year; payback 2.50 years; benefits include speed, accuracy and stock information.
hints: Outlay = software plus training.
Payback = outlay ÷ annual saving.

stem: A fictional furniture factory in Mutare introduced ERP. Before ERP it recorded 120 lost orders a month because materials were out of stock, and each lost order lost US\$8 of profit. After ERP, lost orders fell to 30 a month. Average stock of materials fell from US\$36,000 to US\$24,000, and holding stock costs 15% of its value a year. The system cost US\$27,500 and a support fee of US\$3,500 a year. In the first month, several storekeepers entered receipts wrongly.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit gained in a year from the fall in lost orders.
parts.explanation: Fall in lost orders = 120 - 30 = 90 a month. Profit gained = 90 × 8 × 12 = US\$8,640.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Fall in lost orders = 120 - 30 = 90 a month.
2. Monthly profit = 90 × 8 = US\$720.
3. Annual gain = 720 × 12 = US\$8,640.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual saving in holding costs.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the net annual benefit after the support fee.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether introducing ERP was a good decision for the factory.

points.description: Net annual benefit of US\$6,940 against a cost of US\$27,500: payback of almost four years
Lost orders fell by three quarters, keeping customers
Stock held fell, releasing US\$12,000 of cash
Early errors by storekeepers show the need for training and accurate data
Benefits not counted, such as better costing and management information
Counter-argument: the payback is long and benefits may be overestimated
Judgement with a reason, for example worthwhile in the long run if staff are trained

levels.descriptor: Figures used with the case; benefits, costs and risks weighed; a justified judgement
Some figures and some weighing; judgement weakly supported
General statements about ERP with little use of the case

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The net annual benefit is US\$6,940 against a cost of US\$27,500, so payback is almost four years, which is fairly long. However, lost orders fell by three quarters, keeping customers, stock fell and released US\$12,000 of cash, and benefits such as better costing and information are not counted. The early errors show that staff need training and accurate data entry. Overall the decision was probably worthwhile in the long run, provided the factory trains its storekeepers and the benefits continue.

parts.explanation: Uses the net benefit, the payback and the case facts to reach a judgement.
hints: Calculate the payback and set it against the other benefits and risks.

explanation: Profit gain US\$8,640; holding-cost saving US\$1,800; net benefit US\$6,940; evaluation weighs payback, benefits and risks.
hints: Annual figures need the monthly figure × 12.
Subtract the support fee from the benefits.

stem: A fictional metal-fabrication workshop in Gweru makes gates and window frames to customers' designs. Each new design is drawn by hand and takes two days; changes mean drawing it again. The cutting machines are set by hand. The owner is considering computer-aided design (CAD) and computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) equipment costing US\$16,000.

points.description: CAD uses computers to create and test designs
Application: the workshop could draw and change a gate design on screen
CAM uses computers to control the machines that make the product
Application: the cutting machines could cut metal to the design without being set by hand

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: CAD uses computers to create and test designs, so the workshop could draw and change a gate design on screen. CAM uses computers to control machines, so the cutting machines could cut the metal to the design without being set by hand.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Outline two advantages to the workshop of CAD and CAM.

points.description: Designs can be changed quickly
Application: customers' changes need no redrawing by hand
Cutting is accurate and repeatable
Application: less metal is wasted and gates fit properly
Speed of production rises

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Designs can be changed quickly on screen, so customers' changes need no redrawing by hand. Machine cutting is accurate and repeatable, so less metal is wasted and gates fit properly.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Discuss whether the owner should buy the CAD and CAM equipment.

points.description: Faster design and accurate cutting may win more orders
Lower waste and labour time reduce costs
The cost of US\$16,000 may be large for a small workshop
Workers need training and may fear losing jobs
Counter-argument: orders may not be large enough to justify the cost
Judgement with a reason, for example buy if orders are growing; otherwise start with CAD only

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Faster design and accurate cutting could win more orders and lower waste and labour costs. However, US\$16,000 is a lot for a small workshop, and workers need training and may fear losing their jobs. If orders are not large enough the equipment would not pay for itself. The owner should buy it if orders are growing; otherwise he could start with CAD only.

parts.explanation: A balanced discussion with a reasoned conclusion.
hints: Weigh benefits against cost, and say what the decision depends on.

explanation: Distinguishes CAD and CAM, gives advantages and discusses the purchase in context.
hints: CAD = design, CAM = manufacture.
Use the workshop's facts in each answer.
